batchName: Empire: Diocletian and Constantine (AD 284-337) - Medium Batch 1

questions.question: Maximian took the title 'Herculius' after which figure?
options: Jupiter
Mars
Hercules
Apollo
Mithras
questions.explanation: Maximian took his title from Hercules, Jupiter's heroic helper. The names mirrored the partnership, with Diocletian as Jovian senior and Maximian as his Herculean partner.
questions.sourceQuote: Maximian became *Herculius*, after Jupiter's heroic helper Hercules.

questions.question: According to Constantine's later propaganda, how did he escape from Galerius's court?
options: He climbed the walls during a feast
He sailed away down the Danube by boat
He fled at night, laming the post horses behind him
He slipped out disguised as a travelling merchant
He bribed the palace guards with gold
questions.explanation: Constantine's propaganda said he fled the same night Galerius agreed to release him, laming the post horses so he could not be followed. Galerius had given his consent after an evening of drinking.
questions.sourceQuote: According to Constantine's later propaganda, he fled that night, laming the post horses behind him.

questions.question: Why did the choice of new Caesars in 305 damage the Tetrarchy?
options: The army refused to accept any new Caesars
The Senate in Rome chose its own candidates
Constantine and Maxentius were passed over for Galerius's allies
Maximian refused to resign in Milan
Diocletian named his own sons over proven generals
questions.explanation: The crowd expected Constantine and Maxentius to become Caesars, but two of Galerius's allies were chosen instead. That slight would wreck the system.
questions.sourceQuote: The crowd expected Constantine and Maxentius, Maximian's son, to become Caesars, but two of Galerius's allies were chosen instead, a slight that would wreck the system.

questions.question: Which region, long untaxed, had to start paying taxes under Diocletian?
options: Gaul
Syria
Africa
Egypt
Italy
questions.explanation: Italy had long been spared regular taxes, but under Diocletian it paid too. The money funded a bigger government and an army of some 580,000 men.
questions.sourceQuote: Italy, long untaxed, now paid too.

questions.question: Diocletian's new regular tax was assessed in which units? (select all that apply)
options: Amphorae of wine from each estate
Modii, standard measures of grain
Capita, counting people by heads
Tithes of a tenth of each harvest
Iuga, land units varying with soil and crop
questions.explanation: The tax was assessed on people, counted in capita, and on land, measured in iuga that varied with soil and crop. From 296 a census every five years kept the figures current.
questions.sourceQuote: It was assessed on people, counted in heads (*capita*), and on land, measured in units (*iuga*) that varied with soil and crop.

questions.question: How did Diocletian publicly shame Galerius after the Persians defeated him in 297?
options: He stripped him of his title of Caesar
He demoted him to a cavalry officer
He exiled him to a Danube garrison
He made him walk a mile ahead of the procession
He made him pay for the lost army
questions.explanation: Diocletian made Galerius walk about 1.5 km ahead of the imperial procession in his purple robes. Galerius struck back in 298 and won two great battles.
questions.sourceQuote: Diocletian publicly blamed him, making him walk about 1.5 km (a mile) ahead of the imperial procession in his purple robes.

questions.question: What did the bishops Constantine summoned to Nicaea in 325 produce?
options: A list of banned pagan temples
The Nicene Creed
The Edict of Milan
The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
The first Latin Bible
questions.explanation: The bishops gathered at Nicaea in north-western Turkey and produced the Nicene Creed, a statement of Christian belief. Constantine also funded great churches such as the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
questions.sourceQuote: In 325 he summoned bishops to Nicaea, a town in north-western Turkey, where they produced the Nicene Creed, a statement of Christian belief.

questions.question: By 282, what military post did Diocles hold?
options: Prefect in charge of Egypt
Admiral of the Adriatic fleet
Governor of the province of Dalmatia
Commander of the emperor's household cavalry
Commander of the Danube frontier forts
questions.explanation: By 282 Diocles commanded the cavalry that guarded the emperor's household. He had risen through the army during the Crisis of the Third Century.
questions.sourceQuote: By 282 Diocles commanded the cavalry that guarded the emperor's household.

questions.question: What was the Chi-Rho on Constantine's battle standard, the labarum?
options: A cross set inside the disc of the sun
The initials of Constantine and his father
A Latin abbreviation of 'In this sign, conquer'
The first two Greek letters of Christ's name
An eagle holding a laurel wreath
questions.explanation: The Chi-Rho combines the first two Greek letters of Christ's name. In the bishop's account, Christ told Constantine in a dream to put it on the labarum.
questions.sourceQuote: That night Christ told him in a dream to make a battle standard, the *labarum*, bearing the Chi-Rho, the first two Greek letters of Christ's name.

questions.question: Why did Maxentius leave the safety of Rome's walls to fight in 312?
options: He trusted a prophecy that Rome's enemy would die
Constantine had breached the city walls
His troops mutinied and forced him out
The Senate ordered him to fight
His food supplies had run out
questions.explanation: The Sibylline Books said that 'the enemy of the Romans' would die on 28 October, and Maxentius took this as a promise. He had twice beaten invaders before by holding out behind the walls.
questions.sourceQuote: The Sibylline Books, ancient prophecies kept in Rome, said that on 28 October “the enemy of the Romans” would die, and he took this as a promise.
